title: Chicago jobs: Beach Hotel, Montmartre Cafe, and bringing Santo Pecora up
summary: He joined the Chicago local, worked at a beach hotel and the Montmartre Cafe, and got Santo Pecora a trombone job through the Benson agency, earning good overtime.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I told him, he said, where you from? I said, from here. Oh, man, that's all. He says, man, wait. Meet me tomorrow at the local. Man. Yes, the next morning, the next day I meet him at the local. He introduced me. The brothers brought me. At that time, you know, I don't know if the law is the same now. You had to be in Chicago, Chicago, and then place six months before you could take a study job. Yeah, stuff right now, too. Most places, yeah. Sometimes three months. Yeah, exactly. Well, I have my transfer card. So finally, I brought me into the office, his brother, you know, and everything. So finally, he got some, I can't think, I think the brother's name is Phil Boyd, I think his name was. The only time he was called. He had a banner. He called the beach hotel. Now you know where that's at. Yeah, we're not sure. No, yeah. So I went out there, went to work out there. Stood out there about a month. And going over big. So they called me up at the local. So what they done, took me away from there, they sent me up on Broadway in Lawrence. Used to be the Green Mill one time. At that time it was called the Mont Mont Cafe. I don't know if you remember that. No. I think it's the Arabic call right now. Yeah, I know that. I went up there. Working up there. Who comes in town? Santa Piccararo. I'm home sleeping. He was working in Biloxi with Joe Polko. During the summer, the Palace Theater was closed. You remember that? Yeah. You from the Lawrence? No, I remember the Palace Theater was. So Santa comes up there. I wake, come knocking on my door. I'm sleeping about telegraph in the morning. Where you come from, boy? I just got in town. We had rehearsal that afternoon. I brought Santa. There was a book of the agent. I can't think of his name. I think it was George Edwards. So... Benson. Oh, I'm talking about the soul dog going wrong. There were a lot of Benson bands.
Benson, yeah. Benson officers. Benson, yeah.
I was a booking agent. He had a lot of them, yeah.

So I brought him up there and had to rehearse him and everything. And had a trombone player there. Santa sat in, played a couple of numbers. Man, right away this meeting wanted Santa. Took 15 trombone players. Then five though. Put him on the netted job. So we were working there. We'd go to work at 8 o'clock. To one. Five hours. To the peak north. We'd go to work at 8 o'clock. To one. Five hours. To the peak north. We'd go to about 13 men, 12, 13 men. And after one o'clock. They keep a Dixieland combination. Wow. And we skid overtime. Well, morning afters. They had another trumpet player with me. I can't remember that time. That man. Because it was such a good job. He was a wonderful musician. But he couldn't pay. In Chicago? Yes. Where would he from? Well, the morning after he'd leave. Our salary was $100 a week. But our overtime was to get $180, $170. We'd get $2 an hour overtime. $150. $160. $140. You know what I mean? As long as the people stayed through daylight.
